meta.title: Who really said "Quotation Is a Serviceable Substitute for Wit"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Shaw, and not Wilde. W. Somerset Maugham wrote the line into his story The Creative Impulse for a 1931 collection. Quote Investigator traced it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Quotation Is a Serviceable Substitute for Wit'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces this line to W. Somerset Maugham's 1931 story revision — not George Bernard Shaw, and not Oscar Wilde. The documented trail.

answer.label: Not George Bernard Shaw — actually W. Somerset Maugham
answer.authorDates: 1874–1965 · English novelist, playwright and short-story writer
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the line to Maugham’s short story “The Creative Impulse,” where the version revised for the 1931 collection Six Stories Written in the First Person Singular describes a character: “She had a pretty gift for quotation, which is a serviceable substitute for wit…” The phrase is absent from the story’s first printing in Harper’s Bazar in August 1926, and the tidy standalone epigram passed around under Shaw’s name — and far more often Wilde’s — is a later trimming of Maugham’s sentence, with no evidence either man wrote it.

source.excerpt: She had a pretty gift for quotation, which is a serviceable substitute for wit…
trail: August 1926 — “The Creative Impulse” first appears in Harper’s Bazar. Quote Investigator checked that printing on microfilm and reports that the phrase is not in it ↗.

1931 — Maugham revises and expands the story for Six Stories Written in the First Person Singular (Doubleday, Doran and Company), and the clause is there. QI verified the wording at page 255 of a 1977 Arno Press reprint ↗ of that edition; the 1931 volume itself is digitised at the Internet Archive ↗.

May 1993 — on the Usenet group alt.quotations, one reader asks whether a different variant, “The ability to quote is a poor substitute for wit,” should go to Shaw or to Wilde; a second reader replies with the “serviceable” wording and credits Maugham. That exchange is the only Shaw connection QI documents ↗.

February 1997, then 2007 — the line comes loose from Maugham altogether. QI records a Usenet post crediting Oscar Wilde in February 1997, and by 2007 the compressed form had reached Goodreads, where it is still filed under Wilde with no source given ↗.
source.excerptNote: Maugham wrote the line about a character, Mrs. Albert Forrester, and buried it in a much longer sentence that runs on about her thirty years of distinguished acquaintances and her stock of anecdotes. As Quote Investigator observes, that phrasing was awkward if you wanted a concise stand-alone quotation — which is exactly why later versions trimmed it into an epigram.

author.name: W. Somerset Maugham
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · English novelist, playwright and short-story writer
author.bio: William Somerset Maugham was an English playwright, novelist and short-story writer, born in Paris in 1874 and died at Nice in 1965. He sold on a scale few literary writers reach — four and a half million copies of his books were bought in the United States during his lifetime — and his sharpest lines tend to sit inside his short stories rather than stand alone as aphorisms. “The Creative Impulse” is one of those stories, a piece in which Maugham made fun of self-conscious stylists — which is roughly what the “serviceable substitute for wit” clause is doing there.

misattribution.heading: Four famous names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: For a line about quotation standing in for wit, this one has had an unusually busy career being quoted — under at least three names that are not Maugham’s.

items.why: The phrase does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote’s Shaw page ↗, in its sourced sections or its misattributed ones. The single Shaw link Quote Investigator turned up is a May 1993 post on alt.quotations in which a reader wondered whether a different variant — “The ability to quote is a poor substitute for wit” — belonged to Shaw or to Wilde ↗. A question posted to a newsgroup is not a source.

Wilde, not Shaw, is where this line usually lands today. QI dates the Wilde ascription to a February 1997 Usenet post and finds no substantive evidence Wilde said or wrote it ↗; it is nevertheless still served up as Wilde’s, sourceless, on Goodreads ↗.

An August 1994 Usenet message credited “The ability to quote is a serviceable substitute for wit” to Voltaire ↗. It did not stick, but it shows how freely the sentence travelled once it was detached from its author.

Even the sites that get the author right usually print “The ability to quote is a serviceable substitute for wit,” a rewrite that QI tracks back through 1990s Usenet and a January 1997 newspaper column, not to Maugham’s page. The bare “Quotation is a serviceable substitute for wit” is a further compression again. Wikiquote prints what he actually wrote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Maugham wrote it — not as a maxim, but as a dry aside about a character, in the version of “The Creative Impulse” revised for the 1931 collection Six Stories Written in the First Person Singular. Quote Investigator traced the trail ↗.

context.heading: Why this one drifted
lead: There is a mechanism behind misattribution, and this quote demonstrates it cleanly. Maugham did not write an epigram. He wrote a subordinate clause — “which is a serviceable substitute for wit” — hung off a description of a minor character, inside a sentence that keeps going for another thirty words about her acquaintances and her anecdotes. Nobody can quote that at a dinner party.

So it got trimmed. First into “The ability to quote is a serviceable substitute for wit,” then into the four-word-shorter “Quotation is a serviceable substitute for wit.” And once a sentence has been filed down into an epigram, it needs an epigrammatist. Maugham is a novelist; Wilde and Shaw are professional wits. The line migrated to the men it sounded like.
detailsBody: The 1926-versus-1931 split is the detail that makes this checkable. “The Creative Impulse” ran in Harper’s Bazar in August 1926 without the phrase; Quote Investigator confirmed that on microfilm. Maugham then revised and expanded the story for the 1931 Doubleday, Doran collection, and the clause is in that text, verified by QI at page 255 of a 1977 Arno Press reprint. Any source that pins this line to a Maugham work before 1931 has skipped a step.

Worth noting what the sentence is doing in context. It is not Maugham offering advice about conversation. It is Maugham gently needling Mrs. Albert Forrester, a character whose gift for quotation is being described as a stand-in for a wit she does not have. Read as a maxim it is a tip; read in place it is a barb.
context.pull: A line about quotation substituting for wit, repeatedly quoted under the names of wittier men.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence Oscar Wilde said or wrote the line; a version was in Maugham's 'The Creative Impulse' as revised for the 1931 collection Six Stories Written in the First Person Singular, was NOT in the August 1926 Harper's Bazar printing (verified on microfilm), and the wording was verified at page 255 of the 1977 Arno Press reprint. QI also documents the May 1993 alt.quotations Shaw/Wilde exchange over 'The ability to quote is a poor substitute for wit', the August 1994 Voltaire ascription, a January 1997 Oak Park Oak Leaves column crediting Maugham, a February 1997 Wilde ascription, and the 2007 Goodreads posting.

Wikiquote lists 'She had a pretty gift for quotation, which is a serviceable substitute for wit...' in its sourced Short stories section under Maugham, notes it was 'Revised with quotation in the 1931 compilation Six Stories Written in the First Person Singular', and states it is 'Often misattributed to George Bernard Shaw or Oscar Wilde'. Maugham's dates are given as 25 January 1874 – 16 December 1965.
The phrase 'substitute for wit' / 'serviceable' appears nowhere on Wikiquote's George Bernard Shaw page, including its Misattributed and Disputed sections (0 matches in the full raw wikitext).
The Internet Archive holds a digitised copy of 'Six stories written in the first person singular' by William Somerset Maugham, published by Doubleday, Doran & Co, 1931.

Wikisource's Maugham author page lists Six Stories Written in the First Person Singular (1931) among his short-story collections and states that his works are in the public domain in the United States because they were published before 1 January 1931.
Goodreads displays 'Quotation is a serviceable substitute for wit.' attributed to Oscar Wilde, with no source work cited.

Wikipedia describes W. Somerset Maugham as an English playwright, novelist and short-story writer, born 25 January 1874 in Paris and died 16 December 1965 in Nice; states that four and a half million copies of his books were bought in the US during his lifetime; and says that in 'The Creative Impulse' (1926) Maugham made fun of self-conscious stylists.
